---
title: "Monitoring models"
subtitle: "Monitoring after initial evaluation"
description: "Learn how to measure model performance across time slices and why different labels can make an old score misleading."
categories: [model development, monitoring, model drift]
---

A model passes its initial evaluation, and its API is ready to score paragraphs.

Three months later, the incoming paragraphs differ. Their words and file format
remain familiar, and the deployment record still contains the original score.
Those facts do not establish unchanged performance.

Monitoring examines differences after deployment. It can compare incoming text
with training text. When the team makes sure the labels are correct, monitoring can also measure
prediction performance.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- score a fitted text model across time slices.
- read held-out slice scores without treating them as a new train/test study.
- measure input drift when labels are late or missing.
- explain concept drift in plain language.
- explain why a fixed party text model needs fresh evidence.
- name what monitoring can and cannot see.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Refit the era model

For a monitoring lesson, we replay the corpus as if labeled paragraphs arrived
from different periods. The model is the same penalized logistic regression with
tf-idf features. The split seed is `4301`, and the fit seed is `4302`.

```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tibble)
  library(stringr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(stopwords)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(rsample)
  library(recipes)
  library(textrecipes)
  library(parsnip)
  library(workflows)
  library(yardstick)
  library(broom)
  library(glmnet)
})

source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")
paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()

set.seed(4301)
era_split <- group_initial_split(paragraphs, group = speech_id, prop = 0.75)
era_training <- training(era_split)
era_testing <- testing(era_split)

era_recipe <- recipe(era ~ paragraph, data = era_training) |>
  step_tokenize(paragraph) |>
  step_stopwords(paragraph) |>
  step_tokenfilter(paragraph, max_tokens = 500) |>
  step_tfidf(paragraph)

era_model <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 0) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

era_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(era_recipe) |>
  add_model(era_model)

set.seed(4302)
era_fitted <- fit(era_workflow, data = era_training)

held_out_predictions <- predict(era_fitted, era_testing) |>
  bind_cols(era_testing |> select(era))

held_out_accuracy <- accuracy(
  held_out_predictions,
  truth = era,
  estimate = .pred_class
) |>
  pull(.estimate)

era_length_summary <- paragraphs |>
  group_by(era) |>
  summarise(
    paragraphs = n(),
    median_words = median(paragraph_words),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    item = c("paragraphs", "held-out paragraphs", "held-out accuracy"),
    value = as.character(
      c(nrow(paragraphs), nrow(era_testing), round(held_out_accuracy, 4))
    )
  ),
  col.names = c("Item", "Value"),
  caption = "Model and corpus size for the monitoring replay",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(paragraphs), 1377L),
  identical(n_distinct(paragraphs$president), 40L),
  identical(nrow(era_testing), 335L),
  identical(round(held_out_accuracy, 4), 0.8209),
  identical(as.integer(era_length_summary$paragraphs), c(485L, 892L)),
  identical(as.numeric(era_length_summary$median_words), c(112, 54))
)
```

The held-out score is still the evaluation score. Any slice score below uses
only those `r nrow(era_testing)` held-out paragraphs, never rows from the
training side.

## Score held-out time slices

A **monitoring slice** is a subset assessed separately, such as a month, region,
source, or time period. This lesson uses historical periods. However, the `era`
label comes from year, so time-based slices also separate labels. A slice with
one label measures that class's recall rather than overall performance.

```{r}
period_breaks <- c(1780, 1849, 1899, 1949, 1999, 2030)
period_levels <- c(
  "1789-1849",
  "1850-1899",
  "1900-1949",
  "1950-1999",
  "2000-2025"
)

held_out_by_period <- held_out_predictions |>
  bind_cols(era_testing |> select(paragraph_id, year, paragraph)) |>
  mutate(
    period = cut(
      year,
      breaks = period_breaks,
      labels = period_levels,
      right = TRUE
    )
  )

label_counts <- held_out_by_period |>
  count(period, era, name = "labels") |>
  complete(
    period = factor(period_levels, levels = period_levels),
    era = levels(paragraphs$era),
    fill = list(labels = 0L)
  )

period_accuracy <- label_counts |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    held_out_paragraphs = sum(labels),
    before_1900 = sum(labels[era == "before 1900"]),
    later_1900 = sum(labels[era == "1900 or later"]),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    held_out_by_period |>
      group_by(period) |>
      summarise(
        correct = sum(.pred_class == era),
        accuracy = mean(.pred_class == era),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    by = join_by(period)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    correct = if_else(is.na(correct), 0L, as.integer(correct)),
    score_kind = case_when(
      held_out_paragraphs == 0L ~ "no held-out rows",
      before_1900 == 0L | later_1900 == 0L ~ "one-class recall",
      TRUE ~ "two-class accuracy"
    )
  )

lowest_slice <- period_accuracy |>
  filter(held_out_paragraphs > 0L) |>
  slice_min(accuracy, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  period_accuracy |>
    select(
      period,
      held_out_paragraphs,
      before_1900,
      later_1900,
      correct,
      score_kind,
      accuracy
    ) |>
    mutate(accuracy = round(accuracy, 3)),
  col.names = c(
    "Period", "Held-out paragraphs", "Before 1900 labels",
    "1900 or later labels", "Correct", "Score type", "Accuracy"
  ),
  caption = "Held-out era scores by period with class composition",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(period_accuracy), 5L),
  identical(period_accuracy$held_out_paragraphs, c(67L, 128L, 23L, 117L, 0L)),
  identical(period_accuracy$before_1900, c(67L, 128L, 0L, 0L, 0L)),
  identical(period_accuracy$later_1900, c(0L, 0L, 23L, 117L, 0L)),
  identical(period_accuracy$correct, c(58L, 87L, 17L, 113L, 0L)),
  identical(
    round(period_accuracy$accuracy[!is.na(period_accuracy$accuracy)], 3),
    c(0.866, 0.680, 0.739, 0.966)
  ),
  identical(sum(period_accuracy$held_out_paragraphs), 335L),
  identical(as.character(lowest_slice$period), "1850-1899"),
  identical(lowest_slice$held_out_paragraphs, 128L)
)
```

The lowest held-out slice is
`r as.character(lowest_slice$period)`, with `r lowest_slice$held_out_paragraphs`
paragraphs and accuracy `r round(lowest_slice$accuracy, 3)`. It is not the slice
around 1900. Every nonempty slice contains one class. The table therefore
demonstrates circular monitoring, where the monitoring groups depend on the
variable used to assign the label. It is not a general accuracy report.

The `2000-2025` row is empty because all speeches from that period entered the
training set under seed `4301`. Grouped splitting keeps whole speeches together, so
a period can have no held-out examples even when the full corpus contains them.

## Watch input drift without waiting for labels

Labels often arrive late or remain unavailable. A team can still compare
incoming text with the text used for model fitting. The code treats the 500
model features as the training vocabulary. It measures the share of
non-stopword tokens outside that vocabulary and reports median paragraph length.

This retrospective teaching check uses the full corpus. Most rows helped
select the vocabulary, so the results favour familiar terms. Live monitoring
should assess only later, unseen text.

```{r}
training_vocabulary <- tidy(extract_fit_parsnip(era_fitted)) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  transmute(token = str_remove(term, "^tfidf_paragraph_")) |>
  pull(token)

period_paragraphs <- paragraphs |>
  mutate(
    period = cut(
      year,
      breaks = period_breaks,
      labels = period_levels,
      right = TRUE
    )
  )

period_lengths <- period_paragraphs |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    paragraphs = n(),
    median_words = median(paragraph_words),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

model_stop_words <- tibble(
  word = stopwords("en", source = "snowball")
)

drift_table <- period_paragraphs |>
  select(paragraph_id, period, paragraph) |>
  # Tokenise with an explicit pattern rather than `unnest_tokens()`. The default
  # word tokeniser uses ICU word boundaries, and ICU versions differ between
  # machines, so the same text can yield slightly different token counts on a
  # Linux runner than on a laptop. A stated pattern makes the count reproducible.
  mutate(token = str_extract_all(tolower(paragraph), "[a-z']+")) |>
  select(-paragraph) |>
  unnest_longer(token) |>
  anti_join(model_stop_words, by = join_by(token == word)) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    tokens = n(),
    absent_tokens = sum(!(token %in% training_vocabulary)),
    absent_share = absent_tokens / tokens,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  left_join(period_lengths, by = join_by(period)) |>
  select(period, paragraphs, median_words, tokens, absent_tokens, absent_share)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  drift_table |>
    mutate(absent_share = round(absent_share, 3)),
  col.names = c(
    "Period", "Paragraphs", "Median words",
    "Non-stopword tokens", "Tokens outside 500 features",
    "Share outside 500 features"
  ),
  caption = "Approximate input-coverage checks by period using the training vocabulary",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(training_vocabulary), 500L),
  identical(nrow(drift_table), 5L),
  identical(drift_table$paragraphs, c(220L, 265L, 317L, 371L, 204L)),
  identical(drift_table$median_words, c(149.5, 92, 67, 53, 43)),
  identical(drift_table$tokens, c(19192L, 14562L, 14388L, 10650L, 5579L)),
  identical(drift_table$absent_tokens, c(9900L, 7390L, 7014L, 4972L, 2800L)),
  identical(round(drift_table$absent_share, 3), c(0.516, 0.507, 0.487, 0.467, 0.502)),
  max(drift_table$median_words) - min(drift_table$median_words) > 100
)

drift_alt_text <- paste0(
  "Two line charts by period, both starting at zero. Median words per paragraph ",
  "decrease from ", max(drift_table$median_words), " in the earliest period to ",
  min(drift_table$median_words), " in the latest. The share of non-stopword ",
  "tokens outside the 500 training features stays between ",
  scales::percent(min(drift_table$absent_share), accuracy = 1), " and ",
  scales::percent(max(drift_table$absent_share), accuracy = 1), "."
)

stopifnot(
  identical(drift_table$median_words[1], max(drift_table$median_words)),
  identical(drift_table$median_words[5], min(drift_table$median_words))
)
```

The stop-word list now matches `step_stopwords()` in the fitted recipe: the
Snowball English list supplied by the stopwords package.

The explicit regular expression differs from the fitted recipe's
`step_tokenize()` tokenizer. It makes this lesson reproducible across ICU
versions. However, `absent_share` approximates feature coverage and can reflect
tokenization differences as well as vocabulary drift.

The vocabulary measure varies little partly because it uses a fixed 500-token
list. About half of the non-stopword tokens are outside that list. The share ranges from
`r round(min(drift_table$absent_share), 3)` to
`r round(max(drift_table$absent_share), 3)` across
`r max(paragraphs$year) - min(paragraphs$year)` years. These historical shares
combine training and held-out rows. They are not an out-of-sample drift estimate.

Median paragraph length varies more clearly. It decreases from
`r max(drift_table$median_words)` words in the earliest period to
`r min(drift_table$median_words)` in the latest. Paragraph length also
contributed to the era result in the evaluation lesson.

Before-1900 paragraphs have median length
`r era_length_summary$median_words[era_length_summary$era == "before 1900"]`.
Later paragraphs have median length
`r era_length_summary$median_words[era_length_summary$era == "1900 or later"]`.
A vocabulary-only check would miss that difference.

Neither check requires labels, so both can execute before samples with reference labels arrive.
Neither establishes that the model remains correct. They compare incoming text
with the model's training text. A model can still make serious errors on
familiar-looking input.

```{r}
#| label: fig-input-drift
#| fig-cap: "Input drift checks by period."
#| fig-alt: !expr drift_alt_text
#| fig-height: 5
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"

source("R/lesson-figures.R")

drift_plot <- drift_table |>
  transmute(
    period,
    `Median words per paragraph` = median_words,
    `Share of non-stopword tokens outside the 500 training features` = absent_share
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -period,
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    value_label = if_else(
      str_detect(measure, "^Share"),
      scales::percent(value, accuracy = 1),
      as.character(value)
    )
  )

# Both panels start at zero, so the nearly flat share does not look like a
# large change just because its panel has its own scale. The zero line is the
# only reference line; the labels carry the values.
panel_floor <- tibble(measure = unique(drift_plot$measure), value = 0)

ggplot(drift_plot, aes(x = period, y = value, group = measure)) +
  geom_blank(data = panel_floor, aes(x = NULL, group = NULL)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    colour = lesson_colours[["context"]],
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(colour = lesson_colours[["accent"]], linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = lesson_colours[["accent"]], size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = value_label),
    vjust = -1,
    family = lesson_font,
    size = 9.5,
    size.unit = "pt",
    colour = lesson_colours[["body"]]
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  labs(
    title = "Paragraph length varies more than vocabulary coverage",
    subtitle = "Two label-free input checks for each period of the inaugural corpus. Both panels start at zero.",
    x = "Period",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_lesson(grid = "none") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(drift_plot), 10L),
  identical(
    sort(unique(drift_plot$measure)),
    c(
      "Median words per paragraph",
      "Share of non-stopword tokens outside the 500 training features"
    )
  ),
  !any(drift_plot$value_label %in% c("0%", "0")),
  identical(
    drift_plot$value_label[drift_plot$measure == "Median words per paragraph"],
    c("149.5", "92", "67", "53", "43")
  ),
  max(drift_table$median_words) - min(drift_table$median_words) > 100,
  max(drift_table$absent_share) - min(drift_table$absent_share) < 0.06
)
```

The length pattern varies more than the absent-token share here. Either
difference could require a check in a live system. Neither difference alone
proves that the model is wrong. Each shows an input difference for
a person to examine.

## Watch labels as well as words

**Concept drift** means the relationship between inputs and labels changes over
time. Text changes when writers choose new words. Labels can change too.

The party column in this corpus spans the full address range. A label such as
`Democratic` appears across many decades. That span is not evidence that one
fixed paragraph model can predict party across the collection. The evaluation
result for this recipe and penalty is a measurement warning, not a political
finding.

```{r}
party_range <- paragraphs |>
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year),
    last_year = max(year),
    years_spanned = last_year - first_year,
    parties = n_distinct(party),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

democratic_range <- paragraphs |>
  filter(party == "Democratic") |>
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year),
    last_year = max(year),
    paragraphs = n(),
    speeches = n_distinct(speech_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

party_rows <- paragraphs |>
  filter(party %in% c("Democratic", "Republican"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  bind_rows(
    party_range |>
      transmute(label = "all party labels", first_year, last_year, paragraphs = nrow(paragraphs)),
    democratic_range |>
      transmute(label = "Democratic", first_year, last_year, paragraphs)
  ),
  col.names = c("Label scope", "First year", "Last year", "Paragraphs"),
  caption = "Long time spans in the party labels",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(party_range$first_year, 1789L),
  identical(party_range$last_year, 2025L),
  identical(party_range$years_spanned, 236L),
  identical(party_range$parties, 6L),
  identical(democratic_range$first_year, 1829L),
  identical(democratic_range$last_year, 2021L),
  identical(democratic_range$paragraphs, 471L),
  identical(democratic_range$speeches, 22L),
  identical(nrow(party_rows), 1197L),
  identical(n_distinct(party_rows$president), 31L)
)
```

Monitoring can detect differences in input distributions. It can also detect
lower scores when the team makes sure reference labels are correct. It cannot
find confident errors on questions that nobody examines. Monitoring therefore
needs people to examine a sample of predictions. It also needs dashboards.

## What to remember

- Monitoring starts after a team packages a model or starts to operate it routinely.
- Slice scores can show where performance changes.
- A slice score is not the same as a new held-out evaluation.
- Concept drift can affect words, labels, or the relationship between them.
- Monitoring cannot find errors in rows that no one examines.

Continue to examine model results even when a dashboard has no alerts.
